newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. dominates lucrative Taiwan mobile phone rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. dominates lucrative Taiwan mobile phone rights.

text.p: A local partnership powered by U.S. giant AT&T Corp. was the big winner Monday in a hotly contested sweepstakes for Taiwan's lucrative mobile phone market, winning two key franchises.

Far Eastone Telecommunications, led by Taiwan's Far Eastern Group with AT&T holding 20 percent, was awarded one of two island-wide mobile licences as well as a northern regional franchise covering Taiwan's bustling capital, Taipei.

Altogether, eight franchises were awarded by the Ministry of Transport and Communications, with U.S. telecommunications giants snapping up most of the prizes in a market expected to generate sales of up to $3.6 billion a year after a decade.

"This means the start of a new telecommunications era," Vice-Minister Mao Chih-kuo said after protracted negotiations that officials had hoped to wind up before the end of 1996. "The opening of the market brings more choices and lower prices. We can also expect better service," Mao added. "That is the aim of market liberalisation."
Mobile telephone services is one of several telecommunications sectors liberalised by parliament in January 1996, opening it up for private and limited foreign investment.
Seventeen joint ventures, most girded by western high-tech giants, submitted 42 bids for the new franchises.
Foreign investors can own stakes of up to 20 percent in Taiwan telecom ventures, though under some interpretations of the liberalised law, foreigners can control up to 59 percent.

Pacific Telecommunications Systems, which links Stamford, Conn.-based GTE Corp. with Taiwan computer giant Acer Inc., Pacific Electric Wire & Cable and transport consortium Evergreen Marine, won the second all-Taiwan licence.
KG Telecom, grouping Kansas City-based Sprint with Taiwan's powerful Koo's Group and Microelectronics Technology, won one of six northern, central or southern franchises.
Rounding out the U.S. winners was San Antonio, Texas-based SBC Corp., whose partnership with huge Formosa Plastics Group, Asia Pacific Investment Co., won a regional licence.
Taiwan's Mobitai, linked with the T-Mobil unit of Germany's Deutsche Telecom, won a regional franchise for Europe.
Two regional franchises went to Smartlink, a Taiwan firm led by giant Tuntex, with no big high-tech partner.

Mao said Taiwan could expect to have three to four million more mobile phones once the eight franchises are established, bringing the mobile coverage rate to 25 percent of the public from less than 6 percent now.
The bid process was to have ended in 1996 but Taipei repeatedly delayed planned announcements of its outcome, saying it needed time to review complex foreign ownership levels.

HongKong Telecom left empty-handed on Monday -- a week after reports that Taipei was blocking its bid due to its part ownership by the top overseas investment arm of the communist Chinese government in Beijing, Taipei's arch rival since a civil war split them in 1949.
Mao confirmed that Hongkong Telecom's mainland pedigree was a factor but said it was not a decisive one.
Other high-profile bidders that went away disappointed were Air Touch Communications, of Walnut Creek, Calif., Singapore Telecom and Japan's Mitsubishi.
